questions.q: A detector catches 95% of fraud and falsely flags 2% of legitimate transactions; 0.5% of transactions are fraud. Roughly what fraction of flagged transactions are truly fraud?
questions.explain: Of 100,000 transactions, 475 fraud cases are flagged versus 1,990 false alarms, so 475 / 2,465 is about 19.3%.

questions.q: In Bayes' theorem, what is the 'prior'?
options: The updated probability after seeing the evidence
The probability of the hypothesis before seeing the evidence, such as the base rate
The probability of the evidence if the hypothesis is false
questions.explain: The prior is your starting probability; the posterior is the updated one.

questions.q: What is the base rate fallacy?
options: Ignoring how rare or common an event is overall when interpreting evidence
Dividing by n instead of n - 1
questions.explain: Focusing on the test's accuracy while ignoring the small prior leads to badly overestimating the posterior.

questions.q: Holding the detector fixed, what happens to P(fraud given flag) as the base rate of fraud rises from 0.5% to 5%?
questions.explain: The same detector is far more trustworthy when the event is more common; the lesson computed about 71.4% at a 5% base rate.

questions.q: What key assumption did the 'second alert' update (from 19.3% to about 92%) rely on?
options: That the two alerts are independent given the true status
That the false positive rate is zero
That the first alert was wrong
questions.explain: If both alerts use the same features, their errors are correlated, and the true posterior would be lower than 92%.
